title: Hydrogen Fuel Cell Safety Procedure
text:
Engineering Department – Swarthmore College
Prepared by: Alexander Vasquez-Jaffe
Date: 11/06/2025


This document outlines the safe storage, handling, and operation procedures for hydrogen and related systems used to operate the hydrogen fuel cell in the Engineering Department. Compliance with these guidelines ensures the safety of students, staff, and equipment.



Hydrogen is a colorless, odorless, and highly flammable gas. Due to its low ignition energy and wide flammability range (4%–75% in air), extreme care must be taken when storing, transporting, and using hydrogen. This procedure applies to all personnel handling hydrogen or operating hydrogen fuel cell systems in the laboratory or vehicle testing areas.





- Hydrogen cylinders must be stored in a designated area, such as the hydrogen gas cylinder holder on the equipment cart or another specially designated storage location.
- Cylinders may remain mounted in the hydrogen car if properly secured and not obstructing ventilation or access.
- Store cylinders away from open flames, sparks, and direct sunlight.
- Maintain good ventilation in any area where hydrogen is stored or used.



- Never lift or carry a hydrogen cylinder by the valve or regulator knob.
- Before connecting the tank, verify that the hydrogen regulator screw is loosened and the cylinder valve is closed.
When ready to operate:
1. Attach the regulator securely to the tank.
2. Confirm that the nipple and connector are properly aligned and tightened.
3. Slowly open the cylinder valve while monitoring for leaks.



- Hydrogen is odorless — leaks must be detected using a hydrogen leak detector or soapy water test.
- If a leak is suspected: immediately close the cylinder valve and check that fittings are correctly tightened and oriented before resuming operation.






- If a hydrogen fire occurs:
- Do not use water.
- Use a Class B (flammable gas) fire extinguisher if safe to do so.
- Contact the supervising instructor or laboratory staff immediately.




- Only authorized, trained personnel may handle hydrogen or operate the fuel cell system.
- Personnel must complete hydrogen safety training and review this document before working independently.

Lathe

Insert 1 in stock
Zero out lathe

LENGTH AND DIAMETER

Ask J which speed to use
Want the machine on high
Want something around 1200 

Zero the machine (Z-axis)

Ask J to show you how
Hit the DRO button to get to the right menu
Crack various wheels until connector is under the drill bit
Put tiny piece of paper on the top of the connector
Crank the giant lever on the right side

It looks like this:
(refrain from saying “Wrong lever Kronk”)

Crank lever until you can still pull the piece of paper out but there is a little bit of resistance
Turn the smaller black lever so that it locks

It looks like this:

On the screen hit “Z” and then “abs zero”

Use the wheels to move the connector from under the drill
Rotate the giant lever out and crank until the screen says -0.365 in
Zero the machine (X-axis)

Make sure the drill is a bit away from the connector, turn the machine on
Move the connector so that the drill takes the smallest amount of material off
Zero the screen (same as on Z-axis)

Take material off in small X-axis increments by cranking the Y-axis wheel so that the bit moves back and forth

J suggests going in 0.02 in increments, but I suggest somewhere around 0.04. You just have to make sure everything is tight so that the connector doesn’t rotate when you mill it flat

Take the correct amount of material off

Amount will vary depending on measurements of the individual connector
Leave 0.3 in of a rim for vertical and one sided horizontal connectors
Leave 0.2 in of a rim on each side for a double sided horizontal connector

Repeat on the other side

Make sure connector and block is going on clean, level surface
Make sure connector and block is flush with the clamp
Re-zero X-axis, you do not need to re-zero Y-axis

Use a metal rasp to remove the burrs
The milled connector will look something like this:


OR



Drilling

Use mill machine
Change drill bit from milling to drilling

Will want something that makes a pilot hole and then a ⅜ in drill bit

Mark the correct spot on the flat part of the connector
For one ended pieces

Put the flat part of connector on top of the metal pieces in the clamp

They look like this:

Tighten clamp 
Drill pilot hole, change drill bit, drill actual hole

For double ended pieces

Put the flat part of connector on smaller square aluminium tubes in the clamp

Use as many scrap square tubes as needed to make top clamp-able and flush-ish (try your best)

Use same process as one ended pieces

Storing hydrogen in the hydrogen car: keep it in the storage, to prevent the tank from being tipped over.
Avoid carrying a hydrogen cylinder by the knob.
Make sure both hydrogen regulator (loosen screw valve is closed) and hydrogen tank (tighten knob) valves are closed before opening hydrogen valve
-Hydrogen is extremely flammable, if there is a leak, immediately close hydrogen valve, cause could be the nipple for the regulator-tank connector is not oriented properly
safety using a power supply that plugs into the wall,
-Make sure no metal clamp is touching other metal,
-connect power supply to wall
-make sure it is on and voltage is correct (12v).
-Then press out-on button so no voltage is flowing from power supply and then connect clamps to leads
-make sure no metal in connection is touching other metal
-safety switches, emergency shut off will cut all power, need to unlock the emergency and hit reset button to return power
-emergency button can be hit to cut all hydrogen flow and power, located on the back right (same side as hydrogen tank)

The Shell Eco Marathon, sponsored by Shell Oil, aims to promote the development of vehicles powered by renewable energy or those that make more efficient use of non-renewable resources. The specific competition that Swarthmore will participate in promotes the development of hydrogen fuel as a renewable source of fuel. Hydrogen fuel is still under development, and offers an alternative to current electric vehicles (EVs) by addressing some of the limitations modern EVs face, particularly range. In essence, hydrogen attempts to eliminate the need for a lithium-ion battery in EVs, which are a primary limitation in current era EVs.
Swarthmore College's former Hydrogen Fuel Cell Vehicle (HFCV) was originally designed in 2013 with minor redesigns in the years following. However, due to the changes in the competition, our current vehicle is unfit for racing. In order to race in the upcoming years, a new vehicle and a revitalization of the entire program must occur. title: Lathing
text: I recorded my process for fabricating linkages. My setup at home is different from the shop at Singer, but it may still be useful for club members.

title: Lathing
text:
Preparing the Stock
I bought 12 feet of 1”-diameter 6061 aluminum rod.

Cutting Stock

I started by cutting the length of aluminum rod that would fit in my lathe with a bandsaw. In this case, I cut 12.5” to make 5 end (no tab) members.

title: Lathing
text:
Facing the Stock

When making the first member, I faced the end of the rod using a facing tool.

title: Lathing
text:
Drilling a Center Hole

I then drilled a center hole in the end using a center drill. This allowed me to keep the rod concentric with a live center while cutting. This step was also crucial in order to drill a centered hole with the drill bit later.
I bumped the cutting tool against the freshly faced surface and used it to zero the Y-axis. I then repeatedly bumped the tool against the side of the rod while rotating it around to find the highest point, and zeroed the X-axis there. I found the diameter varied by about 1/100 of an inch, suggesting a slightly non-circular or off-center rod.

title: Lathing
text:
Turning Down

I used a left cutting tool to turn the last ~2” of rod down to 0.74”. I did this because out of the sample pieces I measured, the small diameter never exceeded 0.74”. These parts will likely need to be turned down further and individually fitted to the carbon fiber tubes.
I turned the part down 0.12” and then 0.24” below the original diameter, leaving a diameter of ~0.76”. I then used calipers to measure how much more I had to take off to reach a diameter of 0.74”, and finished turning accordingly.

title: Lathing
text:
Cutting Glue Grooves

I cut glue grooves ⅜” and ¾” from the end of the rod using the same left cutting tool.

title: Lathing
text:
Chamfering

I chamfered the end using this chamfering tool. This will allow it to slip into the carbon fiber tube more easily.

title: Lathing
text:
Hollowing Out the Member

I drilled out the center of the rod using a ⅜” drill bit. For end members, I drilled deep enough to go through the whole member. For others, I drilled to a depth slightly less than 2”.
I then used a deburring tool to deburr the bore.

title: Lathing
text:
Parting Off

Finally, I parted off using a parting tool. The length of stock I kept depended on the type of member. To cut off an accurate length, I held a flat block against the end of the part, bumped the right side of the parting tool against the block and zeroed the Y-axis. This provided an accurate measurement to the rightmost point on the parting tool blade.

Total Lengths:
For end members, I parted off 2.2”.
For short-tab members, I parted off 3.3”.

title: Lathing
text:
Work Holding

I secured the lathed portion of the member in a ¾” collet in a square collet block. The square collet block allows you to easily make two cuts 180 degrees apart.
I used this height-variable support to provide some support to the end of the stock. I’m not sure how much it helped, but it worked for me.

title: Lathing
text:
First Cut

I cut 1” from the end of the stock, 0.365” down from the highest point. I found the highest point by moving the tool across the stock, probing it for the highest point and zeroing the Z-axis there.
The team manufacturing document suggested cutting in increments of 0.02”-0.04”. With this mill, I found I could cut 0.08” at a time with no issues.

The ability to use hydrogen as a fuel source solves many of the problems currently faced by electric vehicles (EVs). Most notably, because hydrogen is such an energy dense material, hydrogen fueled vehicles are able to have much larger ranges in between refueling than their electric counterparts. Additionally, because hydrogen fuel is liquid hydrogen, the time it takes to refuel is significantly shorter than fully charging an electric vehicle. While an EV may take hours to fully charge the battery, a hydrogen fueled vehicle takes mere seconds. In essence, hydrogen eliminates the need for a battery in an eco-friendly vehicle, and thus removes the limitations of the modern-day lithium-ion batteries found in current era EVs.
Swarthmore College's current Hydrogen Fuel Cell Vehicle (HFCV) was originally designed in 2013 with minor redesigns in the years following. However, due to the changes in the Shell Eco Marathon, our current vehicle is unfit for racing. This started with the senior design capstone of Justin Chai and Ben Horvat as well as the work of current junior Jano Vasquez-Jaffe. Instead of the chassis being built out of aluminum, the new vehicle would be built using carbon fiber tubing and aluminum fittings and connectors.
The research I performed over the course of the summer directly followed their progress made during the year. They were able to provide me with a preliminary design for the chassis and a variety of fabrication methods. I am very lucky to be in the position where I am able to continue my work in the upcoming semesters.

Shell Eco-Marathon Hydrogen Vehicle Revitalization Effort
ENGR 090 Final Design Project
Justin Chai ’24 & Benjamin Horvat ’24
Advised By: Professor Carr Everbach
Swarthmore College, Department of Engineering
May 2024
Abstract
This E90 project was focused on designing, assessing, and fabricating components for a new hydrogen-powered vehicle aiming for participation in the Shell Eco-Marathon. By completing this project, we wanted to gain experience in the design of vehicles and vehicle systems with an energy-efficiency-focused design. This includes a reimagining of the materials and methods used to construct the chassis, building out calculation models to understand how design decisions, such as weight changes and material property shifts, affect the overall efficiency of the vehicle, and providing proof of concept vehicle elements like a new rear suspension and hydraulic braking system. Overall, the team concluded that the new chassis should be fabricated using wrapped carbon fiber members with a hybrid aluminum insert and carbon fiber reinforced 3D printed collar system for the joints. Alongside the successes on the chassis fabrication and rear suspension implementation on the current 2018 iteration of the Swarthmore hydrogen fuel cell vehicle, the team was also able to quantitatively conclude that weight reduction is the top priority in increasing our overall fuel efficiency and competitiveness. With all the successes of the E90 considered and the monumental amount of learning that resulted from it, we hope that our work attracts more participants to take part in the Shell Eco-Marathon hydrogen fuel cell vehicle project, and we hope to have laid a good foundation so that future teams can run the Swarthmore vehicle at the historic Indy 500 track.
Introduction
The advent of climate change pressures innovators to explore alternative energy methods beyond conventional renewable sources. As the world grapples with the urgent need to curtail global carbon emissions, transportation becomes a focal point, demanding innovative approaches to increase EV battery efficiency and disrupt industry reliance on natural gas and petroleum. This transportation imperative is emphasized by the transportation sector’s substantial emission contribution, accounting for approximately one-fifth of global carbon dioxide emissions and over a quarter of annual GHG emissions in the United States. [10]
Hydrogen vehicles powered by fuel cells offer a promising avenue for revolutionizing industrial and commercial transportation systems. A transition to hydrogen technology holds particular importance for heavy-duty applications, such as freight trains, cargo ships, or cranes, and the importance of this transition is fortified by the recognition that heavy-duty vehicles, although constituting a small fraction of the global vehicle fleet, contribute significantly to greenhouse gas emissions—23% in the case of the US. [7][15] Moreover, the continued adoption of hydrogen as a fuel could make impressive strides in transportation due to hydrogen’s energy density and versatility, surpassing that of traditional lithium batteries or diesel fuel. This specific characteristic is especially critical for long-haul transportation, where the high energy demands and weight considerations pose significant implementation challenges for alternative energy options. [16]
Taking into account the growing investment in hydrogen and the goals of a successful E90 design project, the Shell Eco-Marathon, which has been challenging students worldwide to design energy-efficient vehicles since 1985, inspired us to pursue a more thought-provoking multidisciplinary E90. [1] The competition seeks to provide students with hands-on experience in mechanical implementations of energy systems while contributing to the broader narrative of sustainable transportation. For this engineering design project, the team will focus on re-developing a Prototype-class hydrogen fuel cell vehicle (HFCV) aligned with the stringent rules of the Shell Eco-Marathon. In past years’ E90 projects, the HFCV teams have modified versions of the vehicle to barely pass the Shell Eco-Marathon’s strict testing standards. However, after reading reflections from past teams and speaking with faculty alongside a comparison of past Shell Eco-Marathon regulations and current rules, the current team decided that it would be best to rebuild the HFCV from the ground up, hoping that this redevelopment would provide a new foundation for future iterations of the vehicle. Especially in the context of Swarthmore, the team believes that the Shell Eco-Marathon provides a unique opportunity to use the many facets of engineering students are exposed to whether through the electrical wiring systems used for the car’s safety systems, structural engineering principles to test material properties and chassis designs, or even system responses through the redesign of both the braking and suspensions systems. The immense amount of specific design constraints and requirements detailed by the Shell Eco-Marathon’s annual regulations provide the perfect project for multiple types of engineering students in different specializations to come together for a bigger unified mission akin to actual engineering projects in a research or industry environment. The complete list of necessary updates and technical inspection requirements can be found in Appendix D. Moreover, this project’s interdisciplinary nature is only further emphasized by the continuously evolving nature of the rules which require redesigns and reassessments of engineering best practices every few years, prompting year-long team projects and multiple E90s. In completing this project, the current team will assess the current vehicle while laying the groundwork for a competition-ready vehicle in the years to come.
Theory
In the past, Swarthmore College has participated in the Shell Eco-Marathon for multiple years. With the rules of the competition constantly evolving to improve safety and to reflect current vehicular challenges, the 2018 HFCV has reached the end of its competitive lifespan. Needed modifications of the existing design include but are not limited to, back suspension, hydraulic brakes, a new vehicle cowl, and many additional safety considerations. With a current base vehicle that has already been modified multiple times, ending in two recent failures, and given the number of changes needed to qualify for the competition, the team is moving forward with a new design from scratch in hopes of more successful participation in years to come. In the following paragraphs, the mechanics of key components of the HFCV will be discussed alongside their implications on the design process.
How Does a Hydrogen Fuel Cell Work
Understanding the mechanics of a hydrogen fuel cell vehicle provides insights into its potential as a sustainable transportation solution. At the heart of this technology lies the Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC), a pivotal component in converting hydrogen into electricity. As pressurized hydrogen enters the anode side of the fuel cell, it undergoes a catalytic process, splitting into H+ ions and electrons (e-). Simultaneously, pressurized oxygen on the cathode side splits into oxygen atoms, each carrying a strong negative charge. The electrons released at the anode side then travel through an external circuit, generating an electric current that powers various components, ultimately returning to the cathode side. [5] Afterward, the hydrogen ions move through an electrolyte membrane that permits only positively charged ions to pass. As a result, on the cathode side, the oxygen atoms attract the H+ ions, forming water (H2O) as a byproduct of the reaction. Figure 1 depicts this hydrogen-to-electricity conversion process.
To harness the electricity produced, individual fuel cells are combined into a stack, connected by bipolar plates. This stack is the power source for the electric motor of the vehicle. The fuel cell stack sends electricity to the motor, allowing it to turn the wheels and propel the vehicle forward.[8] For reference, the fuel cell stack typically used for the Shell-Eco Marathon is the Horizon XP PEM fuel cell which features 30 fuel cells stacked together for an advertised max power of 1000W [17]. This stack implementation showcases the versatility of hydrogen fuel cell technology in delivering power for practical transportation needs as fuel cell units are incredibly small and can compound on top of one another to meet electricity demands compared to battery electric vehicles [18]. See Figure 2 for a diagram of how a fuel cell vehicle’s systems typically interact with each other to propel it forward. [4] The pros of hydrogen fuel cell vehicles are noteworthy. Beyond offering emission-free driving and quick refueling, these vehicles provide an extended range compared to some battery-powered counterparts. However, challenges persist, such as the limited hydrogen fueling infrastructure, high production costs of high-efficiency fuel cells, and unsustainable hydrogen production methods.
Physics of Fuel-Efficient Design
The Shell Eco-Marathon presents a unique racing challenge that diverges from typical racing ideology: how can we create the most fuel-efficient vehicle while maintaining a high level of safety? Despite this challenge being the antithesis of a timed race, we can rely on designs and research on modern race cars to inform our design decisions. One of the most tried-and-true ways to increase fuel efficiency is by reducing weight. Modern-day race cars are composed mainly of carbon fiber systems that make the overall car as lightweight as possible. While the specifics of these racecar systems may not be as cost-effective for our purposes, we still considered our own versions to strive for a near minimum weight in race conditions. In addition, modern aerodynamic research has completely shifted the expectation of drag on race vehicles. provide some sort of baseline aerodynamic body design that can be worked on in the year following. Likely, the body design itself can be a future project as the aerodynamic considerations of the cowl and body shape could be a considerable undertaking, even using Singer Hall’s basement wind tunnel and the open-air wind tunnel in Singer Hall’s High Bay. Nonetheless, we must ensure that the new vehicle’s frame remains flexible while meeting safety requirements.
As our focus will be primarily on mechanical systems attached to the chassis, such as the suspension and brakes, putting in the necessary effort to get all systems right is critical. Suspension systems play a role in both the stability and the energy return when the vehicle faces uneven conditions. Minimizing flex and fatigue in the chassis material will help receive more out of the suspension system and allow it to act more ideally. When designing a successful suspension and steering system, the vehicle must be able to adapt and respond to impulses while also maintaining the reaction of the vehicle to mitigate large amounts of energy loss in the process. With modern Shell-Eco Marathon rules now requiring suspension on the rear wheel, we have taken the opportunity to design the full system to our liking. Explored suspension systems were inspired by modern motorbikes’ telescopic fork suspension, modern Formula One vehicles’ wishbone system, and recumbent trike suspension. Regardless of methods, the interaction between the suspension system and the steering system must be considered to ensure safety and high performance. [11] [19]
Our current vehicle provides a great baseline design to move off of and improve. The single-wheel drive back with cambered wheels provides an excellent efficiency-centric design. New designs keep the general wheelbase design but make necessary adjustments for future developments. These future considerations include the location of the design’s center of gravity, the camber of the front wheels, the framing bracing design for load paths, and the widths of the chassis body. All of this is tantamount to a final fuel-efficient vehicle design. [3]
Strain and Stress on Tubes
When designing a new chassis, it is important to consider the mechanics behind creating a structure out of individual elements. The design process of a chassis is similar to a truss: place members in a manner that distributes force evenly and efficiently to the ground and/or wheels. Typically in truss design, the primary concern is failure in the member in tension or compression, and thus the members are sized accordingly. Additionally, there needs to be consideration of shear capacity when utilizing joinery such as pins. Both of these principles will be the key to our exploration and testing.
The most simple model for how loads are distributed in a chassis would be to imagine the entire structure as a single block or beam with the wheels as pins or rollers. When we place a single load (in our case, the driver) at the midspan of the beam, the beam starts to angle in at the ends: pulling on the bottom fibers and compressing the top fibers to resist the downward load. This helps us understand the general tendency of members of a chassis with the top of the chassis primarily resisting tension and the bottom primarily acting in tension.
If we consider individual joints, it is important to size hardware and materials properly to ensure that unplanned fractures do not occur and compromise the structural integrity of the chassis. When we load a member on a pin, we have to consider the shear capacity of both the material and the pin. Shear can be calculated with the equation below.
\(\tau = \frac{F}{A}\)
Eq 1. τ is the shear stress, F is the force applied, and A is the cross-sectional area in the plane resisting the force
Additionally, the shear modulus can be calculated using the equation below.
\(G = \frac{F/A}{\bigtriangleup x/l} = \frac{Fl}{A \bigtriangleup x}\)
Eq 2. F is force applied, l is initial length (or thickness of medium), A is area of resisting shear, and Δx is displacement
While the pinned joint assumptions are useful to get approximate loads, axial loads are not the only design consideration. Many of our joints will act more as fixed joints than pins as the chassis needs some form of rigidity to be functional. Whenever members are fixed in a truss structure, they often become statically indeterminate and take on internal moments. Hydraulic Brakes 101
As stated in the Shell Eco-Marathon rules, the HFCV must have two hydraulic brakes acting on the two axles of the vehicle. The HFCV, with the driver inside of it, must also be able to come to a full stop with the front and rear brakes, individually, at a 20° incline. These rule changes emphasize the need for a safety update from the current Swarthmore HFCV, a vehicle that still uses mechanical rim brakes. In previous iterations of the vehicle, mechanical rim brakes were rational choices to hydraulic disc brakes because of their easy maintenance and installation, aerodynamic nature, and lighter weight. Furthermore, although the vehicle is incredibly unlikely to be running in wet conditions or high-speed scenarios, mechanical rim brakes are known for sporting reduced energy dissipation after unideal contact with the bike rim, either by slipping or rim deterioration from friction heating [20]. Comparatively, hydraulic disc brake systems are widely adopted in mountain bikes and cars due to their numerous advantages [3]; specifically, the ability to modulate the braking force with minimal effort is particularly advantageous. In cars, hydraulic brake systems provide efficient and reliable braking, contributing to safety and stability. See Figure 4 of the schematic of a disk brake system acting on a standard automobile. [9] 
When the brake pedal is pressed, the master cylinder, acting as the heart of the system, initiates hydraulic pressure by compressing brake fluid [13]. This pressurized fluid is then transmitted through hoses and lines to the brake calipers, which house pistons. Disc brakes, such as the ones depicted in Figure 4, have a rotor attached to the wheel, and calipers with pistons that press against the rotor when hydraulic pressure is applied. This clamping generates friction, slowing or stopping the rotation of the wheel [12]. Because of this disc rotor clamping system, the bike’s braking system is now unattached to the condition of the bike rims, making it more reliable in unideal testing environments. Moreover, since a disc rotor system dissipates friction heating into the metallic disc rotor instead of the bike rim, disc brakes can allow for more severe levels of braking on downhill sections or sudden emergency stops [21]. Although the implementation and installation of these hydraulic brakes required the team to spend more time considering the interaction of the brake’s components with the HFCV’s chassis and wheel systems, the hydraulic brakes are a necessary component to enter the competition and to successfully race the vehicle safely and efficiently.

Tensile Testing with Carbon Fiber Members
Carbon fiber tubes have two common compositions: pultruded and wrapped. Pultruded carbon fiber is constructed by aligning individual strands of carbon fiber along the length of the member. In contrast, wrapped carbon fiber takes various strands of carbon fiber and stacks them on top of each other in layers at different angles to provide a more robust performance. The cost point for a wrapped carbon fiber tube is slightly higher than a pultruded carbon fiber tube, so the performance and other potential benefits against the cost will be weighed throughout our testing.
Carbon fiber is a quasi-isotropic material, meaning that it has the same material properties in some directions while metals like aluminum are isotropic materials. While carbon fiber does act similarly to metal in tension, especially in tension, but compressive behavior of wrapped carbon fiber is difficult to characterize and often not ideal.
When it comes to joining the carbon fiber members together, less traditional methods must be used to have high strength and reliable performance. To solve this problem, often epoxy and a connector are introduced. In our case, we decided to use a high-strength epoxy known as 3M DP420. When researching effective methods of composite joineries, we came across a study that indicated that adding glass beads helped boost epoxy performance. Other ways to boost epoxy performance include adding texture to the mating surfaces along with adding a key, or space for epoxy to fill in and increase shear interaction with itself rather than the surface.
We hypothesized that 3D prints or aluminum would provide a good medium to fix a connection between tubes with aluminum. For aluminum, it seemed more natural and time-efficient to use a machined rod to provide a stronger backbone. On the other hand, the 3D print seemed more efficient to support the outside due to its flexibility. Due to the ability to print tensile collars with the carbon-fiber reinforced filament at the Makerspace through their MarkForged printer, the 3D prints offered an inexpensive method to produce comparative draft designs for the joint connections. As a result, we were able to properly test the effect of different carbon fiber joint connection configurations alongside the standardized insert method. For both of the reasons listed, our first draft designs used an aluminum backbone to connect to the inside and the second design used a 3D print collar to grab the outside of the tube. The CAD designs for the 3D printed designs and the technical drawings for the aluminum inserts can be found in Appendix A.

Rear Suspension Forces and Design
The primary design of a single-wheel lever suspension system consists of a few key connection points: a hinge off of the chassis, the connection of a spring to the arm and the chassis, and a connection of the wheel or wheel axle to the suspension. Measurements were gathered on the existing chassis and motor to ensure the suspension would work on the existing chassis and axle. Chrome moly weldable inserts and steel spherical rod ends were purchased to provide a pivot point where bolted onto the chassis in an aluminum holder. These rod ends are extremely smooth and provide flexibility in the attachment alignment.
In the process of fabrication, there was a realization that the bolt for the suspension would not be able to be fed into the eye of the suspension in its current triangular shape. Additionally, the angles of coping for triangular shapes were extremely difficult to get to proper dimensions. There was a mid-fabrication audible to have a ladder support structure, adding only the weight of another 5” large diameter chrome moly tube. This change gives us the flexibility to use multiple springs on the lever arm while improving the design's maintenance and flexibility. Additionally, the attachment brackets intended to connect the rod end eyes of the suspension to the chassis were intended to be welded aluminum plates, but the large filler rod and the difficult heat behavior of small aluminum pieces proved to make the task impossibly difficult. J. Johnson was incremental in helping CNC the parts out of aluminum blocks to provide the design specifications without needing to weld.
The existing 450 lb/in spring that was used in the current suspension is slightly too small for competition use. The current resting conditions for the chassis result in a large displacement of the spring, and the addition of a sitting driver causes the suspension to make contact with the chassis. Either adding another 450 lb/in spring to work in parallel or getting a stiffer spring may fix this issue. The future vehicle should attempt to provide a ladder attachment point on the top to match the design of the suspension.
Hydraulic Braking Installation 
The hydraulic disc brake system was explored in the latter half of the project to provide documentation for future hydraulic brake installations. As laid out in the methods section for the setup of the brake installation and the necessary parts, the brakes were attached to the rear suspension system using a 3D printed attachment that nested the chydraulic brake calipers. As the disc could be easily mounted onto the rear electric motor wheel, the calipers were able to be mounted with an extremely tight tolerance. The final installation of the piece can be seen in Figure 24. Although quantitative response times were not collected to compare with the mechanical rim brakes, we noted that the current vehicle skidded less upon actioning the lever. Furthermore, future implementation of the hydraulic brakes should ensure that the hydraulic hosing is longer than the purchased 3 feet of housing as the team ran into difficulty during the installation due to its short nature. Nonetheless, the hydraulic brake system was quite easy to install, and we recommend further research to quantitatively assess the brakes while finding proper tires to put new disc brakes onto.
Conclusion & Future Considerations
For the last eight months, the team was able to realize massive strides of progress in the effort to revitalize the Shell Eco-Marathon HFCV. Although the original aspirations of competing in the 2024 Shell Eco-Marathon were cut short in the early stages of the project due to the realization of the monumental amount of work needed, we were able to sift through past reports, begin research on foreign-to-Swarthmore topics like carbon fiber joinery, design new mechanical systems for the chassis, brakes, and suspension, and provide a strong playbook that outlines numerous interdisciplinary mini-projects. We also want to acknowledge the immense design project that the Shell Eco-Marathon is, and we have outlined in the following paragraphs our design struggles and our recommendations to circumvent those design struggles.
Our final chassis system design is intended to use a combination of both 3D printed and aluminum joinery. The chassis is sectioned in two primary planes or rectangles stacked on each other to form a similar tub to the original design, with the aluminum insert design acting as a strong backbone in tension, compression, and moment resistance. The vertical and diagonal frames can be connected using 3D-printed collars and aluminum or steel bolts to connect and reinforce the relationship between the two planes. Given that the 3D print was able to resist well beyond the minimum design load, we are confident that the 3D prints will be able to reliably resist any compressive or tensile load that it may face. The combination of the two joinery strategies allows the user to get in and out of the vehicle without concern while still prioritizing the safety and weight of the vehicle.
There are also multiple projects we believe should be progressing simultaneously to the chassis fabrication, albeit at a lower priority. Nonetheless, these systems are still integral to the vehicle’s efficiency and overall ability to pass the Eco-Marathon technical inspections. The highest priority after the chassis fabrication and front suspension changes is undoubtedly the inclusion of pedal brakes and a new steering system. Although progress was made in both systems through our work with the hydraulic brake trials on the current vehicle and the installation of a new steering column that barely passes the Shell Eco-Marathon rules on turning radius, both explorations in this E90 are rudimentary and far from the competition ready versions we envision in 1-2 years. The hydraulic braking system will need to be installed on the front wheels which require us to replace the drum brakes and the front trike tires completely, and because we need to have the front brakes readily accessible by a foot pedal, there will be necessary research on bleeding hydraulic brakes and how to action them with a pressure pedal. We envision that the research, design of the brake pedal, and implementation of the brakes onto new front wheels could be an entire side project that a student could take on. Additionally, the current steering column hosts an array of issues that can endanger the driveability of the HFCV. Because of its rigid design structure using two tie rods attached to the suspension kingpin attachments, any attempt to steer the vehicle while moving results in heavy vibrations throughout the vehicle. The steering column and handle essentially drag the wheels in a direction that makes the steering bumpy and unresponsive. A future project could focus on researching and designing a tire-knuckle system for the new front wheels, and both the braking team and steering team could work jointly on building a new tire hub system for the new vehicle.
As we ran short on time, we were unable to redesign the front suspension for the vehicle. We believe that using the same principles from the current suspension design, commonly known as a wishbone suspension, we should be able to recreate the same system but lighter in chrome moly tubing or, at minimum, aluminum plating. Given that the front wheels also need hydraulic brakes, a full rehaul of the wheel and brake system must be considered as part of that design and thus the current design must be at least modified to meet competition standards. To fully consider and successfully design a solution would likely require a large amount of labor and trial and error to ensure that the next solution only improves and does not detract from overall performance. This would make a great E90 for anyone interested in suspension or braking design and response.
Secondary to the mechanical systems of the car are the cowl and aerodynamic projects. Since the nature of the Shell-Eco Marathon competition is an efficiency project, the aerodynamic design of a cowl, floor, and external features is an integral nature of keeping the Swarthmore vehicle competitive. Although our project did not have time to explore the aerodynamics of the vehicle, we were able to gather information on the aerodynamic designs of other competition vehicles which could inform this project. As a big portion of the current project focuses on how to use carbon fiber members to fabricate the chassis, we would recommend the pursuit of a carbon fiber sheeted cowl. This cowl would likely be in the shape of an inverse airfoil to create downforce on the floor of the vehicle and allow us to deftly cut through the airflow in front of the vehicle. The aerodynamic project could also focus on working with the chassis fabrication team to decrease the frontal area and method for how the driver should be sitting as most competition vehicles now feature a reclined seating arrangement similar to Formula 1 race cars. As the floor design can also impact how the car grips the track and we are given strict guidelines on the dimension of the vehicle’s clearance from the ground, it could also be interesting for the aerodynamics team to work with the chassis fabrication team on the best designs for the floor.
Finally, the safety and electrical systems are projects that we believe should be explored later in the vehicle development process. Besides more mechanical fabrications such as the roll cage, floor, crumple zone, and mandatory firewall, the electrical system requirements such as the emergency shutdown switch, hydrogen regulator, horn, and startup system are currently satisfied by the current electrical design of the vehicle. Key upgrades for the electrical system include a cleanup of the electrical system through rewiring, an addition of a supercapacitor to provide the necessary energy to jumpstart the vehicle when necessary, and a revamp of those ignition and safety buttons near the driver. Otherwise, the 2019 Horizon H-1000 Fuel Cell was still serviceable, and the electrical system worked mostly as intended. However, a side project that may be interesting for the electrical team during the beginning of the design of the new vehicle could be the redesign of the circuitry and the fuel-cell-hydrogen-tank rear area. We have sketched out a potential redesign in Appendix C.
Ultimately, multiple possible projects can assist in making a new HFCV competition ready for the Shell Eco-Marathon, and although we have not highlighted all the design constraints that must be considered for the final vehicle, we have been able to chip away the information and research barrier that can hinder future teams from pursuing these projects. The full set of design constraints and additional minor rules can be found in Appendix D.
Acknowledgments
There are too many people to thank for their contribution and support. Whether you supported us through the construction of our experiments, brainstorming the new designs for the joint connectors and rear suspension, or hearing us discuss for hours why the fuel cell might not be working, we genuinely appreciate your thoughtfulness and assistance.
Namely, we would love to thank the Engineering faculty and staff members who went above and beyond to ensure that we had the adequate resources and knowledge to tackle such an immense project. Our advisor, Professor Carr Everbach, was a champion of the project, and he gave us so many resources and ideas every week that we do not think the project would have turned out as well without him. J. Johnson had to endure the worst of it: hearing us throw out the most outrageous fabrication ideas in the beginning stages of the project, teaching us how to properly use a plethora of machine shop equipment, and pulling through for us and going the extra distance throughout the entire suspension and the joint connectors fabrication process. Truly, J does not deserve enough praise for all he does for everyone in the engineering department. Cassy Burnett was amazing for helping us get materials in such a timely fashion and sorting through shipping woes, and we wish her well in her retirement.
Finally, we would love to thank Jano Vasquez-Jaffe who kept the project alive until both of us joined the project for our E90. He is truly passionate about the hydrogen fuel cell project, and we know that his curiosity and love for automobiles will engage new students in the competition for years to come. The project is in good hands with him and Professor Everbach at the helm. To all our friends and family as well, the journey to complete this project has been long, but it has been one of the most enriching engineering challenges both of us have had the opportunity to work on.
Good luck to all future members of the Eco-Marathon team in making your dreams and ours a reality! Thank you all for your support!

Shell Eco-Marathon Hydrogen Vehicle Revitalization Effort
ENGR 090 Proposal to Investigate Vehicle Redesign
Justin Chai ’24 & Benjamin Horvat ’24
Advised By: Professor Carr Everbach
Swarthmore College, Department of Engineering, December 2023
Project Overview
This E90 project is focused on designing and fabricating components for a new hydrogen-powered vehicle aiming for participation in the Shell Eco-Marathon. By completing this project, we aim to gain experience in the design of vehicles and vehicle systems with energy-efficiency-focused design. More specifically, we hope to gain experience in materials testing, suspension mechanics, and renewable energy system implementation with the vision of a revamped hydrogen fuel cell vehicle. We hope that our work attracts more participants to the competition team and paves the way for more successful competition participation in 2025.
Introduction
The advent of climate change pressures innovators to explore alternative energy methods beyond the realm of conventional renewable sources. As the world grapples with the urgent need to curtail global carbon emissions, transportation becomes a focal point, demanding innovative approaches to increase EV battery efficiency and disrupt industry reliance on natural gas and petroleum. This transportation imperative is emphasized by the transportation sector’s substantial emission contribution, accounting for approximately one-fifth of global carbon dioxide emissions and over a quarter of annual GHG emissions in the United States. [10]
Hydrogen vehicles powered by fuel cells offer a promising avenue for revolutionizing industrial transit systems and commercial vehicles alike. The transition to hydrogen technology holds particular importance for heavy-duty applications, such as freight trains, cargo ships, or cranes, and the importance of this transition is fortified by the recognition that heavy-duty vehicles, although constituting a small fraction of the global vehicle fleet, contribute significantly to greenhouse gas emissions—23% in the case of the US. [7][14] Moreover, the continued adoption of hydrogen as a fuel could make impressive strides in transportation due to hydrogen’s energy density and versatility, surpassing that of traditional lithium batteries or diesel fuel. This specific characteristic is especially critical for long-haul transportation, where the high energy demands and weight considerations pose significant implementation challenges for alternative energy options. [15]
Taking into account the growing investment in hydrogen and the goals of a successful E90 design project, a notable initiative is the Shell Eco-Marathon, which has been challenging students worldwide to design energy-efficient vehicles since 1985. [1] The competition’s mission not only seeks to provide students with hands-on project experience in mechanical implementations of energy systems but also contributes to the broader narrative of sustainable transportation. For this engineering design project, the team will focus on re-developing a Prototype-class hydrogen fuel cell vehicle (HFCV) aligned with the stringent rules of the Shell Eco-Marathon. In past years’ E90 projects, the HFCV teams have modified versions of the vehicle to barely pass the Shell Eco-Marathon’s strict testing standards. However, after reading reflections and speaking with faculty, the current team decided that it would be best to rebuild the HFCV from the ground up, hoping that this redevelopment would provide a new foundation for future iterations of the vehicle. Moving forward, the proposal will detail the technical background of HFCVs, including the physics of the fuel cell stack, hydraulic braking mechanisms, chassis design, and suspension mechanics. The proposal will also detail the timeline, budget, qualifications, and milestones the team hopes to achieve by the end of the project. The team is looking forward to completing an operational framed HFCV by May, and they hope to gain the necessary technical expertise to lay the foundation for future Swarthmore Eco-Marathon teams. The team is looking forward to completing the planning, design, and implementation of several systems and subassemblies that lay the foundation for future Swarthmore Eco-Marathon teams.
Technical Discussion
Swarthmore College has participated in the Shell Eco-Marathon in multiple years past. With the rules of the competition constantly evolving to improve safety and overall performance, our current design has reached the end of its competitive lifespan. Needed modifications of the existing design include back suspension, hydraulic brakes, crumple zones, and hands-free systems. Given the number of changes needed to qualify for competition on a base that has already been modified multiple times and failed to qualify the last two times prior, the team is moving forward with a new design from scratch in hopes of more successful participation in years to come. In the following paragraphs, the mechanics of key components of the HFCV will be discussed alongside their implications on the design process.
How Does a Hydrogen Fuel Cell Work:
Understanding the mechanics of a hydrogen fuel cell vehicle provides insights into its potential as a sustainable transportation solution. At the heart of this technology lies the Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC), a pivotal component in converting hydrogen into electricity. As pressurized hydrogen enters the anode side of the fuel cell, it undergoes a catalytic process, splitting into H+ ions and electrons (e-). Simultaneously, pressurized oxygen on the cathode side splits into oxygen atoms, each carrying a strong negative charge. The electrons released at the anode side travel through an external circuit, generating an electric current that powers various components, ultimately returning to the cathode side. [5] The hydrogen ions move through an electrolyte membrane, designed to permit only positively charged ions to pass. On the cathode side, the oxygen atoms attract the H+ ions, forming water (H2O) as a byproduct of the reaction.
To harness the electricity produced, individual fuel cells are combined into a stack, connected by bipolar plates. This stack is the power source for the electric motor of the vehicle. The fuel cell stack sends electricity to the motor, allowing it to turn the wheels and propel the vehicle forward. [8] This implementation showcases the versatility of hydrogen fuel cell technology in delivering power for practical transportation needs. See figure 2 for a diagram on how a fuel cell vehicle’s systems typically interact with each other to propel it forward. [4] The pros of hydrogen fuel cell vehicles are noteworthy. Beyond offering emission-free driving and quick refueling, these vehicles provide an extended range compared to some battery-powered counterparts. However, challenges persist, such as the limited hydrogen fueling infrastructure, higher production costs, and energy-intensive hydrogen production methods.
Physics of Fuel-Efficient Design:
The Shell Eco-Marathon presents a unique racing challenge that diverges from typical racing ideology: how can we create the most fuel-efficient vehicle while maintaining a high level of safety? Despite this challenge being the antithesis of a timed race, we can rely on designs and research on modern race cars to inform the design decisions we make. One of the most tried-and-true ways to increase fuel efficiency is by reducing weight. Modern-day race cars are composed mainly of carbon fiber substitute systems with the intention of making the overall car as lightweight as possible. While these systems may not be as cost-effective in our case, we may still consider our own versions or the implication of certain driving systems in weight where necessary as we strive to be near minimum weight in race conditions. In addition, modern aerodynamic research has completely shifted the expectation of drag on race vehicles. provide some sort of baseline aerodynamic body design that can be worked on in the year following. Likely, the body design itself can be its own year of exploration, so we must ensure that the frame remains flexible while meeting safety requirements.
As our focus will be primarily on suspension and brake design in supplement to the chassis, it is critical that we put in the necessary effort to get both systems right. Suspension systems play a role in both the stability and the energy return when the vehicle faces uneven conditions. Minimizing flex and fatigue in material that makes up the chassis will help receive more out of the suspension system and allow it to act more ideally. When designing a successful suspension and steering system, the vehicle must be able to respond to impulses and adapt for handling, but also not deaden the reaction of the vehicle so much that there are large amounts of energy loss in the process. With competition rules now requiring suspension on the rear wheel, we have the opportunity to design the full system to our liking. We may opt to use the suspension system from the existing vehicle or find prepackaged systems meant for bicycles/trikes given the similarity to our design. Regardless of methods, the interaction between the suspension system and the steering system must be considered to ensure safety and high performance. [11]

Our current design provides a great baseline design to move off of and improve. The single-wheel drive back with the chambered wheels provides an excellent efficiency-centric design. We plan to keep the general wheelbase design but make any necessary adjustments for newer developments. Potential changes include: location of the design’s center of gravity, camber of front wheels, framing bracing design for load paths, and widths of the chassis body. Research will be done during the design phase to help inform most of the changes, and research of best methods for hydraulic brakes and suspension will be continually researched before they are eventually implemented. [3]
Despite this car being primarily for the Shell Eco-Marathon, we want to also explore biomechanical design to make the previous car flexible enough to take on large passengers. This decision is rooted in trying to make the car more interactive and exciting to a rising generation of Swarthmore Engineers. The current car is designed specifically for someone who is lightweight and approximately 5’2”, and having a specific driver constraint creates a need for someone who fits the strict constraints for any potential testing or tuning. By adjusting the base frame to support larger individuals as well, we hope to allow a greater number of people to ride in the vehicle and get excited about hydrogen cars. This does not mean that we are conceding with trying to place first in the competition; we anticipate that the new competitive race body will likely have the same driver limitations. By making the previous car flexible with who drives it, we hope a foot-in-the-door effect will take place and invigorate more Swatties to want to take part in this project in the years to come.
Hydraulic Brakes 101:
As stated in the Shell Eco-Marathon rules, the HFCV must have two hydraulic brakes acting on the two axles of the vehicle. This is to increase overall safety while providing a modern update on the reliability and future-proofness of competition-grade vehicles. A hydraulic disc brake system operates on the principle of converting mechanical force into hydraulic pressure to achieve efficient and reliable braking. The system is composed of key components such as the master cylinder, brake calipers, brake pads, brake rotors, and hoses/lines. [13] When the brake pedal is pressed, the master cylinder, acting as the heart of the system, initiates hydraulic pressure by compressing brake fluid. This pressurized fluid is then transmitted through hoses and lines to the brake calipers, which house pistons. In the case of disc brakes, the calipers contain pistons that exert pressure on brake pads, causing them to clamp onto the brake rotor. This clamping generates friction, slowing or stopping the rotation of the wheel. There are different types of hydraulic brakes, with disc brakes being a common and efficient choice. [12] Disc brakes, such as the one described above, have a rotor attached to the wheel, and calipers with pistons that press against the rotor when hydraulic pressure is applied. They are known for their superior stopping power and effective heat dissipation. Another type is the drum brake, where hydraulic pressure is applied to wheel cylinders that push brake shoes against the inside of a drum. While less common in modern vehicles, drum brakes are still used in specific applications. 
Hydraulic brake systems are widely adopted in mountain bikes and cars due to their numerous advantages. [3] In mountain biking, where precise and powerful braking is crucial, hydraulic disc brakes offer superior stopping power, allowing riders to navigate steep and challenging terrains with confidence. The ability to modulate the braking force with minimal effort is particularly advantageous. In cars, hydraulic brake systems provide efficient and reliable braking, contributing to safety and stability. The even distribution of weight among all tires, quick adjustments during emergencies, and the minimal effort required on the brake pedal enhance overall driving safety. See Figure 4 of the schematic of a disk brake system acting on a standard automobile. [9] The reliability, superior performance, and adaptability of hydraulic brake systems make them a standard choice for both mountain bikes and cars, ensuring effective control and increased safety on the road or trail. Although the implementation and installation of these hydraulic brakes will require the team to spend more time considering the interaction of the brake’s components with the HFCV’s chassis and wheel systems, the hydraulic brakes are a necessary component to enter the competition and to successfully race the vehicle safely and efficiently.
Project Plan
Objective: Before E90 final presentations, the team plans to deliver design recommendations for a new hydrogen fuel cell vehicle that satisfies the mechanical constraints set by the 2024 Shell Eco-Marathon rules alongside efficiency and performance comparisons with the current vehicle. The design recommendations will allow future team members to iterate on fabrication and calculations at a faster rate and provide a foundational approach for any future design considerations imposed by changes to the Shell Eco-Marathon Prototype-vehicle rules.
Primary design considerations that we hope to resolve include wheelbase and wheel chamber, chassis material and attachments, suspension and hydraulic brake interaction, and interaction of suspension subassemblies with future chassis. We also hope to gather information on existing conditions on the previous vehicle such as current weight and fuel cell performance. Finally, we will likely provide basic human constraints within the vehicle wheelbase to help inform aerodynamic research during the summer of 2024.
Main Design Constraints: Below, the major design constraints of the design project are listed. These constraints range from resource constraints to physical rules and standards set by the Shell Eco-Marathon for a Prototype-class hydrogen fuel cell vehicle.

Timeline: The E90 design project’s semester-long timeline acts as the project’s biggest constraint. As a result of the time constraints in conjunction with the team’s machine shop experience and ability, the scope of the project was narrowed down to specific mechanical foundations for the hydrogen vehicle. This was decided to make sure that proper attention could be given to the new chassis, brakes, and suspension systems.
Hydrogen Fuel Cell Stack: The current hydrogen fuel cell stack is a 2019 model of Horizon’s H-1000 Fuel Cell stack. [6] As this fuel cell was purchased with the intention to be an integral part of Swarthmore’s next iteration of the Shell Eco-Marathon HFCV, the fuel cell will likely not be replaced and will be a constraint on the potential power and energy that will power the vehicle.
Dimensional Constraints: There are strict dimension requirements for the Eco-Marathon Prototype-class vehicle. The vehicle’s maximum height must be less than 1m, and its track width (measured from the midpoints of one tire to the opposite) must be a minimum of 0.5m. The wheelbase(length between a tire on one side to the tire in front/behind it) must be at least 1m. The ratio of the height and track width must be less than 1.25, and the vehicle’s width must not exceed 1.3m. The maximum vehicle length should not exceed 3.5m; furthermore, the dimensions cannot be achieved by appendages or singularities attached to the main chassis of the vehicle.
Safety Constraints: Safety constraints include a 10cm crumple zone at the front of the vehicle, an adequate bulkhead/firewall to separate the driver and electronic systems, and a roll bar that extends at least 50 mm around the driver’s helmet when seated. The roll bar must also extend in width beyond the driver’s shoulder and withstand a load of 700N. These safety requirements will mostly be used in design recommendations for future teams.
Steering Constraints: As specified by the Shell Eco-Marathon rulebook for Prototype-class vehicles, the HFCV must have front-wheel steering only. The turning radius must be 8 meters or less, and the external wheels of the vehicle must be able to follow a 90° arc of 8 meters in both left and right directions.
Braking Constraints: The HFCV must have two hydraulic braking systems, one per axle, and no brakes acting on the tires directly are permitted. Furthermore, the front brake(s) must be operated by a single foot pedal accessed by the driver, and the rear brake(s) must have a single lever action attached to the front brake pedal or the steering handles.
Weight Constraints: The maximum weight of the vehicle without the driver is 140kg.
Project Budget Constraints: The maximum budget afforded to engineering seniors for this E90 project is $800 which limits the amount of materials testing and iteration that may occur throughout the project.

Relevant Experiences:
Ben has primarily focused his engineering electives on structural engineering with a mix of other disciplines. During the summer of 2022, Ben worked at a general contractor firm as an estimator in a small-scale construction wing where he also gained experience as a designer and scheduler. One project that involved constraint-oriented design was a competitive bid for the design, estimation, and scheduling of a kayak facility to be floating on the Allegheny River in Pittsburgh, PA. He has spent time working on EV vehicle-to-grid charging models during his REU at the University of Michigan-Dearborn and an externship at Turo alongside Swarthmore alumni, Nida Osei, focusing on EV policy and charging infrastructure research.
